title: English Vocabulary 4 · Units 15–16
description: Advanced vocabulary for birth, ageing and death across medical, formal and informal registers, and for rewarding pursuits, leisure interests and social activities.
sourceNotice: Prepared for personal study with the user-provided published reference material used to select teaching targets. Translations, explanations and example sentences were written independently; the original passages, activities and illustrations are not reproduced.

audit.scope: Unit 15 (A–C and Language help), exercises 15.1–15.4 and answer key; Unit 16 (A–B and Language help), exercises 16.1–16.5 and answer key.
audit.pronunciation: Broad British IPA is given for individual words where sufficiently confident. Phrases and variants without a reliable entry-level transcription have empty IPA; no connected-speech pronunciation is invented.
audit.languagePolicy: Learner-facing text and metadata are in English; Brazilian Portuguese appears only in pt fields.
audit.reviewMethod: Checked the complete teaching pages, Language help, exercises and corresponding answer key in the supplied PDF. Reviewed medical terminology, distinctions among death-related registers, leisure-related word choice and phrasal-verb patterns. Authored new examples and translations, then programmatically checked schema, units, IDs, required fields, provenance and Word TTS targets. Browser import and audio playback were not tested.
audit.limitations: No recorded MP3 assets are bundled. Browser-based VocabLab import, Word/Sentence TTS and speech recognition have not been tested. Language concerning medical care, legal inheritance, and housing is presented as vocabulary usage rather than clinical or legal guidance; register labels identify dated or offensive terms.

units.title: Unit 15 — Birth and death: from cradle to grave
units.source: Vocabulary study targets from published reference material; Unit 15. Page information, if available, is retained in sourceAudit.
units.category: People and relationships · birth, ageing, bereavement, legal register
learningObjectives: Use accurate terms for pregnancy and birth while distinguishing everyday from medical register.
Describe ageing, funerals and remembrance with appropriate sensitivity.
Choose condolence expressions and euphemisms suitable for the situation.
Distinguish journalistic and legal death vocabulary and inheritance verb patterns.

sectionsChecked: A · At the beginning (pregnancy, birth terminology and Language help)
B · At the end (ageing, funerals and mourning)

items.example: Her pregnancy was confirmed during a routine appointment.
items.note: The state or period of being pregnant; not the same as conception, the point at which a pregnancy begins.

items.example: She discovered she was pregnant shortly after moving house.
items.note: Adjective: be pregnant; pregnancy is the corresponding noun.

items.example: My colleague is expecting a baby early next year.
items.note: In this sense expect is used in the progressive: is expecting a baby, not expects a baby.

items.pt: estar grávida; estar esperando um bebê
items.example: The couple announced that they were expecting.
items.note: A natural, less clinical way to say someone is pregnant; the continuous form is standard.

items.example: The information leaflet describes the stages following conception.
items.note: Biological term for the beginning of pregnancy, often used in medical explanations.

items.example: The researchers explained how an egg can be fertilised in a laboratory.
items.note: British spelling: fertilise; American English fertilize. The past participle is fertilised.

items.example: A fertilised egg begins to divide into more cells.
items.note: The adjective describes an egg after fertilisation; British spelling is fertilised.

items.example: The diagram shows an embryo at an early stage of development.
items.note: Early developmental stage; later in pregnancy the term foetus is used.

items.example: After fertilisation, the embryo may implant in the lining of the womb.
items.note: In this biological context the embryo implants in the uterus; elsewhere the verb also means insert an object.

items.example: The doctor showed the couple an image of the baby in the womb.
items.note: Everyday term for uterus; more common in ordinary conversation than the medical term.

items.example: The scan showed the position of the uterus clearly.
items.note: Anatomical and medical term for womb; plural uteri or uteruses.

items.example: They sought specialist advice after trying to conceive for a year.
items.note: In reproduction, conceive commonly means become pregnant; elsewhere it can mean form an idea.

items.example: Some couples conceive naturally after fertility treatment has stopped.
items.note: Contrasts conception without assisted reproductive procedures and medical assistance.

items.example: The specialist discussed whether fertility drugs might be appropriate.
items.note: Drugs used as part of some fertility treatments; the expression names the treatment, not a guarantee of conception.

items.example: Age can affect fertility, although individual circumstances vary.
items.note: Noun corresponding to fertile; fertility drugs and fertility tests are common combinations.

items.example: After considering their options, they decided to ask about IVF.
items.note: Initialism for in vitro fertilisation; the English initialism is IVF, whereas Portuguese often uses FIV.

items.example: The clinic offered clear information about in vitro fertilisation.
items.note: Formal name of IVF; British spelling is fertilisation, American fertilization.

items.pt: bebê concebido por fertilização in vitro; bebê de proveta
items.example: The museum display mentioned the first test-tube baby born in 1978.
items.note: Older popular expression for a baby conceived through IVF; today IVF-conceived baby is often more neutral and precise.

items.example: The midwife explained how the foetus develops during pregnancy.
items.note: British spelling: foetus; US spelling: fetus. The book distinguishes it from embryo by development stage.

items.example: The placenta provides a link between the mother and the developing baby.
items.note: An organ that helps transfer nutrients and oxygen during pregnancy.

items.example: She went into labour during the early hours of the morning.
items.note: Fixed British expression: go into labour, not go to labour. US spelling: labor.

items.example: Her labour began earlier than the hospital had anticipated.
items.note: Here labour means childbirth contractions and delivery process, not employment.

items.example: The maternity team discussed whether they should induce labour.
items.note: Medical phrase for starting labour using interventions.

items.pt: ter o trabalho de parto induzido
items.example: She was induced after discussing the options with her clinician.
items.note: Passive construction referring to medical induction of labour, not the everyday sense of induce.

items.example: The team explained how the induction would be monitored.
items.note: Noun from induce; can also refer to orientation or induction in other fields.

items.pt: dar à luz; ter um bebê
items.example: She gave birth to a healthy baby girl last spring.
items.note: Use give birth to a baby; not give a birth.

items.example: The family celebrated the birth of their second child.
items.note: Noun; give birth is the corresponding verbal expression.

items.example: A midwife supported the family throughout the delivery.
items.note: A trained maternity professional; in some countries their clinical scope differs.

items.example: An experienced obstetrician delivered the baby safely.
items.note: In this context deliver means assist a birth; the baby is the object, not a parcel.

items.example: The team discussed recovery after a caesarean delivery.
items.note: Noun referring to childbirth; natural/vaginal and caesarean delivery are distinct terms.

items.example: The consultant recommended a caesarean section after assessing the risks.
items.note: British spelling caesarean; US cesarean. Commonly shortened to C-section.

items.example: The leaflet explained options for a natural delivery.
items.note: Term appears in the exercise; usage varies and can be ambiguous, so vaginal birth is often more precise.

items.word: live to a ripe old age
items.pt: viver até uma idade bastante avançada
items.example: Her grandmother lived to a ripe old age and stayed active for decades.
items.note: Conventional expression for a long life; ripe normally modifies old age here.

items.example: My late uncle was a passionate amateur photographer.
items.note: Placed before a deceased person’s name or relationship; not late meaning delayed.

items.example: The local club organises weekly events for pensioners.
items.note: Especially British English: someone receiving a pension, frequently an older retired person.

items.example: After she retired, she moved into sheltered accommodation near her family.
items.note: UK term for housing providing some support, often for older adults, while preserving independence.

items.pt: trêmulo e cambaleante pela idade; de andar inseguro
items.example: The writer was annoyed when reporters described him as doddery.
items.note: Informal and often patronising or disparaging when applied to older people.

items.pt: senil; supostamente confuso pela idade (termo ofensivo)
items.example: The journalist was criticised for calling the elderly politician gaga.
items.note: Offensive age-related slang; included for recognition, not recommended to describe people.

items.word: have all your wits about you
items.pt: estar com a mente afiada; manter plena lucidez
items.example: Despite the exhausting journey, she still had all her wits about her.
items.note: Idiom for being mentally alert and responsive; pronoun changes with the subject.
items.speechText: have all your wits about you

items.example: The charity provides support to families affected by dementia.
items.note: Medical term for a syndrome affecting memory and other thinking abilities; not a synonym for ordinary ageing.

items.example: The funeral took place in the village church.
items.note: The event or ceremony marking someone’s death.

items.example: The family chose a wooden coffin for the ceremony.
items.note: Container for a dead person before burial or cremation.

items.example: Friends gathered at a wake to share memories of their colleague.
items.note: In UK usage often a gathering after a funeral; in other communities wake may refer to a vigil before the funeral.

items.example: He updated his will after his second child was born.
items.note: Legal noun for a document setting out a person’s wishes regarding their estate.

items.example: The family kept his ashes until the memorial gathering.
items.note: The remains after cremation; used as a plural noun in this sense.

items.example: The town observed a day of mourning after the disaster.
items.note: Mourning is the expression of grief, not morning (time of day).

items.pt: lamentar uma morte; estar de luto
items.example: Hundreds of people gathered to mourn the victims.
items.note: Verb: mourn somebody or mourn a death; mourners are those expressing grief.

items.pt: pessoas enlutadas; participantes de um funeral
items.example: Mourners arrived quietly before the memorial service.
items.note: People who are mourning; not the same as the word morning.

items.pt: enlutado; que perdeu alguém por morte
items.example: The organisation offers counselling to bereaved families.
items.note: A person is bereaved after the death of someone close; the adjective is respectful and appropriate in support contexts.

items.example: Her family chose cremation rather than burial.
items.note: Process of cremating the body; contrasts with burial.

items.example: The ceremony was held at the local crematorium.
items.note: Building or facility where cremation takes place.

items.example: The family arranged a small burial ceremony.
items.note: Placing a dead body in the ground or a grave; contrasts with cremation.

items.example: They planned to scatter her ashes in a peaceful garden.
items.note: Fixed combination for dispersing ashes; local rules for locations may apply.

items.example: Please accept my condolences on the loss of your mother.
items.note: Formal and respectful expression of sympathy; on introduces the loss.

items.word: I was so sorry to hear of your loss
items.example: I was so sorry to hear of your loss, and I am thinking of your family.
items.note: Gentler conversational expression of sympathy than a formal condolence formula.

items.example: Her grandfather passed away peacefully last winter.
items.note: Common euphemism for die, suitable when discussing a death sensitively.

items.example: She told us that a close friend had passed on.
items.note: Euphemism for die; usage can carry spiritual overtones depending on context.

items.example: The old document referred to the poet as having passed over.
items.note: Less common euphemism than pass away; can sound dated or spiritual.

items.example: He looked as though he was at death’s door after the exhausting trek.
items.note: Highly informal and often hyperbolic; avoid using casually about someone with a serious illness.

items.pt: nas últimas; quase sem condições de funcionar
items.example: My old printer is on its last legs and needs replacing.
items.note: Informal idiom often used for worn-out devices; can also describe a very exhausted person.

items.example: Officials confirmed three fatalities following the crash.
items.note: News/reporting term counting deaths caused by an incident, unlike injuries or casualties more broadly.

items.example: Several passengers perished when the ship sank.
items.note: Formal or journalistic for die, especially in accidents or disasters; commonly occurs without passive be.

items.example: The report stated that civilians had been slaughtered in the attack.
items.note: Very strong term for violent killing, not a neutral synonym for die.

items.example: The lawyer contacted the relatives of the deceased.
items.note: Formal/legal nominal expression referring to the person who has died.

items.example: She bequeathed her book collection to the town library.
items.note: Formal/legal: bequeath something to someone, or bequeath someone something.

items.pt: legado; bem ou quantia deixada em testamento
items.example: The museum received a substantial bequest from a former patron.
items.note: Noun for what a person leaves in a will; not a request.

items.example: He inherited a small cottage from his grandmother.
items.note: Use inherit something from someone, not inherit someone something.

items.example: The siblings agreed to use their inheritance to fund a scholarship.
items.note: The money or possessions passed on after a death, or the process of receiving them.

items.example: When the owner died intestate, the estate was distributed according to the law.
items.note: Legal term: intestate means without a valid will.

items.example: The estate was handled under intestate succession rules.
items.note: Legal adjective or adverb connected with death without a valid will.

units.title: Unit 16 — Free time: relaxation and leisure
units.source: Vocabulary study targets from published reference material; Unit 16. Page information, if available, is retained in sourceAudit.
units.category: Leisure and lifestyle · pursuits, hobbies and informal self-descriptions
learningObjectives: Contrast rewarding, fruitful, lucrative, therapeutic and time-consuming pursuits.
Recognise informal labels for leisure preferences without overlooking their connotations.
Use take up, go off, be into, be hooked on and get up to in natural constructions.
Discuss social commitments and distinguish active participants from spectators.

sectionsChecked: B · Informal expressions: how people spend their leisure and Language help

items.example: Volunteering at the shelter has been deeply rewarding.
items.note: Positive experiences or a sense of personal fulfilment, not necessarily financial gain.

items.example: Our weekend writing sessions proved fruitful for both authors.
items.note: Produces worthwhile results; unlike lucrative it need not earn money.

items.example: Her small photography business became surprisingly lucrative.
items.note: Refers specifically to making significant money, not emotional satisfaction.

items.example: He finds long walks therapeutic after stressful meetings.
items.note: Helps emotional or physical wellbeing; it need not be a formal medical treatment.

items.example: Listening to instrumental music is relaxing after work.
items.note: Describes an activity that reduces tension; unlike relaxed, describes the thing causing the feeling.

items.example: The sound of rain had a calming effect on her.
items.note: Emphasises a peaceful effect, often on emotions or an anxious person.

items.example: Preparing the costumes was rewarding but time-consuming.
items.note: Describes activities requiring substantial time; not the same as stressful or unpleasant.

items.example: What began as a hobby eventually became a lucrative pursuit.
items.note: Pursuit can mean a regular activity or interest, not just the act of chasing something.

items.pt: abrir mão de uma noite livre
items.example: She gave up two evenings a week to rehearse with the orchestra.
items.note: Here give up means sacrifice free time for an activity or commitment.

items.example: He does voluntary work at a community garden every Saturday.
items.note: Work done without payment, often for a charitable or community purpose.

items.section: B · Informal expressions: how people spend their leisure
items.example: My sister is a culture vulture who never misses a new exhibition.
items.note: Playful informal label for someone enthusiastic about the arts and culture.

items.pt: pessoa sedentária que passa muito tempo diante da TV
items.section: B · Informal expressions: how people spend their leisure
items.example: During the holidays I turned into a couch potato and watched films all day.
items.note: Informal and often joking or mildly critical label for very inactive leisure habits.

items.section: B · Informal expressions: how people spend their leisure
items.example: She is an amateur astronomer who volunteers at the observatory.
items.note: Someone pursuing an activity for interest rather than as a profession; need not mean unskilled.

items.section: B · Informal expressions: how people spend their leisure
items.example: He used to play as an amateur but is now a professional cyclist.
items.note: Contrast with amateur: someone paid to do an activity or working in it professionally.

items.pt: pessoa que experimenta várias atividades sem se aprofundar
items.section: B · Informal expressions: how people spend their leisure
items.example: He is a dabbler who tries a new craft almost every month.
items.note: Often mildly critical: someone who does an activity superficially or only briefly.

items.pt: experimentar uma atividade sem se aprofundar
items.section: B · Informal expressions: how people spend their leisure
items.example: She dabbled in photography before taking up sculpture.
items.note: Verb pattern dabble in something; implies casual involvement, not expert dedication.

items.section: B · Informal expressions: how people spend their leisure
items.example: He took up a new hobby to meet people after moving abroad.
items.note: Take up means begin regularly doing an activity; commonly take up a sport, instrument or hobby.

items.section: B · Informal expressions: how people spend their leisure
items.example: I prefer finishing my chores before meeting friends at the weekend.
items.note: Routine, necessary tasks, commonly household chores.

items.section: B · Informal expressions: how people spend their leisure
items.example: The neighbours usually mow the lawn on Saturday mornings.
items.note: Fixed collocation; mow is the verb for cutting grass with a mower.

items.pt: pessoa viciada em compras; comprador compulsivo
items.section: B · Informal expressions: how people spend their leisure
items.example: Her friends jokingly call her a shopaholic because she loves sales.
items.note: Informal, often light-hearted term; unlike clinical descriptions, it should not imply a diagnosis.

items.pt: pessoa que trabalha em excesso; viciado em trabalho
items.section: B · Informal expressions: how people spend their leisure
items.example: His colleagues called him a workaholic because he never took a holiday.
items.note: Formed with -aholic by analogy; can be jokey but may imply unhealthy working habits.

items.section: B · Informal expressions: how people spend their leisure
items.example: She jokingly describes herself as a chocaholic and keeps chocolate in her desk.
items.note: Playful, informal coinage; not a medical label.

items.pt: pessoa com dependência de álcool; alcoólatra
items.section: B · Informal expressions: how people spend their leisure
items.example: The leaflet explains why alcoholic is a serious label rather than a playful nickname.
items.note: The book contrasts this with casual -aholic words; avoid trivialising alcohol dependence.

items.pt: muito envolvido com; bastante interessado em
items.section: B · Informal expressions: how people spend their leisure
items.example: These days he is heavily into trail running.
items.note: Informal: be heavily into a hobby or interest; refers to substantial involvement.

items.pt: deixar de gostar de; perder o interesse em
items.section: B · Informal expressions: how people spend their leisure
items.example: I went off competitive gaming once it started feeling like work.
items.note: Go off something means stop liking it; different from an alarm going off.

items.pt: começar a praticar; passar a se dedicar a
items.section: B · Informal expressions: how people spend their leisure
items.example: She took up swimming to improve her fitness.
items.note: Take up a hobby or sport = start; not the same as go off something.

items.pt: isolar-se; ficar trancado longe das pessoas
items.section: B · Informal expressions: how people spend their leisure
items.example: He locked himself away all afternoon to finish his painting.
items.note: Reflexive expression for withdrawing from others for a period of time.

items.section: B · Informal expressions: how people spend their leisure
items.example: They are completely hooked on the new detective series.
items.note: Informal: be hooked on an activity or topic; can signal enthusiasm or dependence.

items.section: B · Informal expressions: how people spend their leisure
items.example: What did you get up to while you were on holiday?
items.note: Informal phrase for what someone did, sometimes implying mischief.

items.pt: vida social agitada; cheia de compromissos
items.section: B · Informal expressions: how people spend their leisure
items.example: Between rehearsals and clubs, she leads a hectic social life.
items.note: Hectic suggests a busy, sometimes exhausting, schedule.

items.section: B · Informal expressions: how people spend their leisure
items.example: I have a full diary this week, so could we meet on Friday?
items.note: British English: diary can mean an appointments calendar, not only a private journal.

items.pt: participante entusiasmado; alguém que participa ativamente
items.section: B · Informal expressions: how people spend their leisure
items.example: He is a keen participant in the neighbourhood chess club.
items.note: Keen conveys enthusiasm; a participant actively joins an activity.

items.section: B · Informal expressions: how people spend their leisure
items.example: Every participant received a programme before the event.
items.note: Contrasts with spectator, who watches rather than takes part.

items.section: B · Informal expressions: how people spend their leisure
items.example: She prefers being a spectator to competing herself.
items.note: Person watching a sporting or other event without directly taking part; contrasted in exercise 16.3.

items.section: B · Informal expressions: how people spend their leisure
items.example: Local residents organised community activities during the festival.
items.note: Activities intended for people in the local community; common with take part in or participate in.

items.section: B · Informal expressions: how people spend their leisure
items.example: He worked on the model railway for hours on end.
items.note: Intensifies the duration of an activity, often suggesting surprisingly many hours.
